title: Haydn's The Creation at Symphony Hall, Nov. 5-7
dek: The Boston Symphony Orchestra and Philippe Jordan perform Haydn's oratorio Nov. 5, 6 and 7 at Symphony Hall on Massachusetts Avenue.
body: Joseph Haydn's oratorio The Creation, based on the Genesis story, returns to Boston: this week the Boston Symphony Orchestra brings it to Symphony Hall for the first time since 1998.
## The work and the cast

Haydn composed The Creation late in his life for soloists, chorus and orchestra, drawing on the Genesis account of the world's making. The BSO places it at the opening of a two-part Creation festival that runs through Nov. 14, part of its season-long exploration of faith and spirituality in music.

Philippe Jordan conducts. Three soloists make their BSO debuts: soprano Louise Alder, tenor Bogdan Volkov and bass-baritone David Steffens. The Tanglewood Festival Chorus, prepared by Jean-Sébastien Vallée, the BSO's Director of Choruses, carries the great choral moments. The text is sung in German with English supertitles, so there is no need to know the language.
## Dates and times
There are three performances at Symphony Hall: Thursday, Nov. 5 at 7:30 p.m.; Friday, Nov. 6 at 1:30 p.m.; and Saturday, Nov. 7 at 8 p.m.

Each night has a companion event, with its own separate ticket. On Thursday, Robert Hazen and Mike Wong give a 6:30 p.m. talk titled Time's Second Arrow in the Cabot-Cahners Room. On Friday, Teresa Neff offers a half-hour talk at 12:15 p.m. in the hall. On Saturday, Christian Wiman and Tracy K. Smith give a 6:30 p.m. reading in the Cabot-Cahners Room.
## Tickets

Symphony Hall is at 301 Massachusetts Avenue, Boston. The BSO lists single-ticket links for each performance on its event page, though it does not publish single-ticket prices there. Subscription packages that include this concert start at $231 and run up to the thousands, depending on the series and seats. For help, call the BSO ticketing office at 617-266-1200 (Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; Saturday, 12:30 to 4:30 p.m.) or email customerservice@bso.org.
The BSO's next orchestral concerts pair this oratorio with a brand-new work, the Golijov Creation.

title: Arlington Open Studios Brings 80 Local Artists to Town Hall and Maple Street
dek: Saturday, November 7 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Arlington Town Hall, the Arlington Community Center and Robbins Library in Arlington.
body: Arlington Center for the Arts presents the 28th annual Arlington Open Studios on Saturday, November 7, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., a town-wide showcase of work by more than 80 local artists. Painters, photographers, fiber artists, ceramicists, glass artists, jewelers, printmakers and sculptors all take part, and most visitors can buy work directly and meet the people who made it.

The day spreads across three connected stops. Arlington Town Hall, at 730 Massachusetts Avenue, has more than 40 artists on two floors, and the Arlington High School Band plays on the Town Hall steps from noon to 4 p.m. The Arlington Community Center and the Arlington Center for the Arts, at 27 Maple Street, hold a second group of more than 40 artists on the ground and first floors, plus a ceramics demonstration from noon to 4 p.m. in the ACA Clay Studio. Robbins Library, at 700 Massachusetts Avenue, adds live readings from the Red Letter Poets.
## Galleries, puppets and food

Two exhibitions give the day a second layer. The Shaira Ali Gallery shows "Opposites Attract," and the Hallway Gallery shows "Inside ACA." Puppet performances by Margaret Moody and friends are scheduled for younger visitors, and The Roasted Granola sells food at the Maple Street entrance. Admission is no charge.

A town-wide open studio day is one of the best ways to meet the artists behind the work you see on gallery walls. The day falls on a single Saturday, so it is worth mapping out which buildings to see before you set out.

title: Igor Levit Brings an All-Beethoven Recital to Symphony Hall
dek: Sunday, Nov. 8 from 3 to 5 p.m. at Symphony Hall, 301 Massachusetts Ave., Back Bay.
body: Pianist Igor Levit makes his Symphony Hall recital debut on Sunday, November 8, with an all-Beethoven program that the presenter, Vivo Performing Arts, describes as a portrait of the composer's inner life. The recital runs from 3:00 to 5:00 p.m.

The program traces a path from the young Beethoven's confident swagger, through the despair that came with his encroaching deafness, to a moment of reprieve and the Waldstein Sonata. That sonata, written around 1803 and 1804 and dedicated to the patron Count Ferdinand Ernst von Waldstein, is one of the composer's most ambitious works for piano and a staple of the repertoire.

Levit has performed with the Boston Symphony Orchestra before, but this is his first recital in Symphony Hall under the Vivo banner. The listing frames the afternoon as a statement of faith in the power of art, and an all-Beethoven program lets listeners follow one composer's arc from beginning to end.
## Getting Tickets

The listing does not spell out every work on the program, so check the event page for the complete set before you go. Single tickets went on sale in August, and Vivo's Applause Circle membership offers early access to tickets. Details, availability and the program are at https://www.vivoperformingarts.org/productions/igor-levit-2026
Symphony Hall is in Back Bay, a short walk from Symphony station on the Green Line. Arrive a little early to find your seat and enjoy the hall before the first note.

title: Poiesis Quartet Plays Beethoven and Prokofiev at the Gardner, Nov. 8
dek: Sunday, Nov. 8, from 1:30 to 3:30 p.m. in Calderwood Hall at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way in the Fenway.
body: The Poiesis Quartet performs in Calderwood Hall at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum on Sunday, Nov. 8, from 1:30 to 3:30 p.m. The concert is part of the museum's Fall 2026 Weekend Concert Series, which runs on select Sundays from Sept. 13 through Nov. 22.
## The program

The listing names four works: Beethoven's final string quartet, Prokofiev's String Quartet No. 1, Sky Macklay's Many Many Cadences, and Tapestry of the Beloved Beatified by Jeff Scott, which the listing describes as a new commission. The mix runs from Beethoven's last quartet to a new commission, a span of about two centuries.
## The ensemble

The quartet was founded in 2022. According to the event listing, The New York Times named it among the best classical performances of 2025, and the group has quickly drawn attention in classical music.
## The hall and the series

Calderwood Hall is a 300-seat room, and the listing notes that about 80 percent of its seats are front row. The Weekend Concert Series dates to 1927 and, according to the listing, is the longest-running museum music program in the country. The concert fills most of a Sunday afternoon, and the listing gives the address as 25 Evans Way, Boston, MA 02115.
## Tickets and details

Tickets are listed at $70 to $99. Seniors pay $63 to $89, and students and children ages 5 to 17 pay $25. The museum's listing for the concert is at gardnermuseum.org/calendar/poiesis-quartet-20261108. Visitors who want the full set of details can also find them on the Boston Calendar page for the concert, which repeats the start and end times.

title: The 48th Boston International Antiquarian Book Fair Opens at the Hynes
dek: Friday, November 6 through Sunday, November 8 at the Hynes Convention Center in Back Bay, with about 110 rare book dealers.
body: The 48th Boston International Antiquarian Book Fair opens on Friday, November 6, at the Hynes Convention Center in Back Bay and runs through Sunday, November 8. About 110 rare book dealers are bringing first editions, manuscripts, maps and autographs, and they travel to Boston from the Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Serbia, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and 24 states.

Hours are 4 to 8 p.m. on Friday, noon to 7 p.m. on Saturday and 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Sunday. A Friday ticket costs $25 and is good for all three days, Saturday is $15 and Sunday is $10. Students and children 12 and under are admitted at no charge, and librarians and staff of nonprofit cultural institutions can register in advance with an organizational email address.
## For new collectors

The fair is a good place to start. The dealers have set aside "Discovery" items priced at $100 or less for people who are just beginning to collect, so a visit can be as much a lesson as a shopping trip. A walk along the aisles puts handwritten pages and early printed books in front of you that are rarely seen outside a museum.
Check the fair's own pages before you go for the current dealer list and any schedule changes.

title: Boston Lyric Opera Opens 'A Streetcar Named Desire' This Week
dek: Thursday, Nov. 5 and Friday, Nov. 6 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, Nov. 8 at 3 p.m. at the Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre on Tremont Street.
body: Boston Lyric Opera opens André Previn's A Streetcar Named Desire at the Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre this week, with performances on Thursday, November 5 and Friday, November 6 at 7:30 p.m. and a matinee on Sunday, November 8 at 3 p.m. The opera sets a libretto by Philip Littell to Tennessee Williams' Pulitzer Prize-winning play. This production is a new co-production with Opera Theatre of Saint Louis and is sung in English with English supertitles.
## A Summer in New Orleans

The story unfolds during a sweltering New Orleans summer. Blanche DuBois moves in with her sister Stella and brother-in-law Stanley, and her romantic view of the past meets his blunt realism. Previn's score gives that meeting a lyrical voice, which makes the opera a fine introduction for anyone who knows Williams' play and for anyone who has never seen it.
## The Company
Daniela Candillari conducts, and Patricia Racette directs. Brittany Renee sings Blanche, Angela Yam sings Stella, Thomas Glass sings Stanley and Brenton Ryan sings Mitch.
## Performances and Tickets

The Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre is at 219 Tremont Street in Boston. Tickets are sold through Boston Lyric Opera's online ticketing page, and the company also offers a general ticketing link for the rest of its season. Arrive a few minutes early to find your seat before the performance begins.

title: Troy Roberts Quartet Plays Arrow Street Arts Tonight, Nov. 9
dek: Monday, Nov. 9, at The Studio at Arrow Street Arts, 2 Arrow Street in Cambridge, with doors at 6:30 PM and music at 7:30 PM.
body: Troy Roberts, a GRAMMY-nominated saxophonist based in New York City, brings his quartet to Cambridge tonight for a jazz evening at The Studio at Arrow Street Arts. Roberts, an Australian immigrant, is a prolific bandleader with sixteen releases to his name, and he has recorded with artists including Joey DeFrancesco, Van Morrison and Kurt Elling.

His latest album is Green Lights, which features John Patitucci, Paul Bollenback and Jimmy Macbride. Tonight's lineup is Roberts on saxophone, Devin Thai on piano, Lois Majors on bass and Austin McMahon on drums.
## The evening

The show is presented by the New England Jazz Collaborative with Arrow Street Arts. Doors open at 6:30 PM, and the music runs from 7:30 to 9:30 PM, according to the event page. The Studio is at 2 Arrow Street in Cambridge, Massachusetts, so the concert suits a weeknight outing for anyone who wants a small room and a full quartet sound.

The orchestra has played this hall before. The group's own website lists a November 2025 concert at the Berklee Performance Center on Massachusetts Avenue, so this evening continues a relationship between the ensemble and the college's main stage.

body: Journey brings its Final Frontier Tour to TD Garden on Tuesday, Nov. 10, billed as an evening with the band, meaning no opener and a long set from the arena-rock giants.

The fall leg added 40 more North American dates to the tour, and Boston is one of them. For a band whose catalog doubles as the soundtrack of a few generations of road trips and ballgames, a full evening means plenty of room for the deep cuts as well as the singalongs.
## Who's on stage

Founding guitarist Neal Schon leads the lineup with longtime keyboardist and guitarist Jonathan Cain and lead singer Arnel Pineda. Deen Castronovo is on drums and vocals, with Jason Derlatka on keyboards and vocals and Todd Jensen on bass and vocals. Drummers in the house will want to keep an eye on Castronovo, who has long pulled double duty behind the kit and on the mic.

title: Nemanja Radulović and Double Sens Make Their U.S. Debut, Nov. 13
dek: Friday, Nov. 13, at 8:00 PM at NEC's Jordan Hall, 30 Gainsborough Street, in the Fenway neighborhood of Boston.
body: Serbian-born violinist Nemanja Radulović, who makes his home in Paris, brings his Double Sens Chamber Orchestra to Boston for a U.S. debut on Friday, Nov. 13. The concert, presented by Vivo Performing Arts, starts at 8:00 PM in NEC's Jordan Hall, and the listing sets the evening from 8:00 to 10:00 PM.

The listing describes the evening as moving between classical masterworks and folk traditions. It names no individual works, and it notes that the program was changed for an earlier performance, so check the Vivo performance page for the current repertoire before the concert.
## A soloist and an ensemble on one stage

Radulović performs as the soloist with the Double Sens ensemble, a format in which the violin line and the orchestra share the stage. Chamber orchestras of this kind are a natural setting for a violinist who moves between concert repertoire and folk material, because the smaller forces let the solo voice sit clearly inside the texture.

Jordan Hall, the NEC concert hall at 30 Gainsborough Street, is built for chamber music. Its acoustics suit string ensembles, and audiences who come to hear a soloist in a room this size tend to hear every shift in dynamics. For a U.S. debut, the hall offers a close, attentive setting.
## Tickets and details

An Applause Circle membership, $25, gives early access to tickets, with details at vivoarts.org/applause-circle. The concert starts at 8:00 PM on Friday, Nov. 13. ## Disreputable Classical Music

The group calls its sound 'disreputable classical music,' a phrase that suits a band that does not let genre labels decide what it plays. Its repertoire draws on classical, contemporary and fiddle music. The group says it wants to bring instrumental music into livelier rooms, and it describes its playing as if the music could be taken away after the show.
## A Room With a History

Club Passim has been a listening room for decades. Its early years as Club 47 drew folk performers including Joan Baez and Bob Dylan, and the room has since welcomed songwriters and acoustic musicians from many traditions. A show there is an intimate way to hear a band up close.

title: Golijov's Creation: a BSO World Premiere, Nov. 12-14
dek: Eric Jacobsen conducts the new Golijov, Hwang and Cohen work Nov. 12, 13 and 14 at Symphony Hall, 301 Massachusetts Ave.
body: A new large-scale work by Osvaldo Golijov is an event in itself. When the Boston Symphony Orchestra presents his Creation at Symphony Hall, it will be a world premiere commissioned by the orchestra, and the culminating event of the BSO's Creation festival.
## An answer to Haydn

Golijov, the Argentine-born American composer, wrote the music. David Henry Hwang, the Tony Award-winning playwright who wrote the libretto for Golijov's opera Ainadamar, supplies the book, and Leah Hager Cohen the lyrics. The BSO describes the piece as a response to Haydn's oratorio The Creation, which the orchestra performs the week before. The BSO says it explores the cosmos alongside human cruelty and tenderness, and asks what it means to answer the call to create.
The BSO compares its scale to Golijov's La Pasión según San Marcos, and WCRB reports that the music draws on jazz, Arabic and Brazilian traditions.
## The performers

Eric Jacobsen, in his BSO conducting debut, leads the orchestra and the Tanglewood Festival Chorus. Vocalist Cécile McLorin Salvant and bass-baritone Davóne Tines are featured, joined by percussionist Cyro Baptista and Kayhan Kalhor on the kamancheh. The BSO x NEC Honors Children's Choir takes part, and the staging includes original artwork and animation by Alex Sopp and projection design by Camilla Tassi.
## Dates, tickets

Performances are Thursday, Nov. 12 and Friday, Nov. 13 at 7:30 p.m., and Saturday, Nov. 14 at 8 p.m. Before the Saturday concert, at 6:30 p.m. in the Cabot-Cahners Room, Golijov speaks with the physicist and novelist Alan Lightman; this conversation is open to ticket holders for the 8 p.m. performance, and the BSO also asks for a separate RSVP because space is limited.

Symphony Hall is at 301 Massachusetts Avenue, Boston. Single tickets are sold through each performance's link on the BSO event page, which does not list individual prices. Phone 617-266-1200 or email customerservice@bso.org for help.
New music, a distinctive instrumental lineup and a question as old as Genesis make this one of the season's most talked-about nights in Boston.

title: Boston Baroque's X-tet Sings Songs of Italy on Nov. 13 and 14
dek: Friday and Saturday, November 13 and 14, at Seully Hall in the Boston Conservatory at Berklee, with soprano Amanda Forsythe.
body: Boston Baroque's string ensemble, the X-tet, returns this month with a program its own announcement describes as a sweeping celebration of Italian baroque and Renaissance music. The concerts take place on Friday, November 13 and Saturday, November 14, in Seully Hall at the Boston Conservatory at Berklee.

The evening opens a window onto the Italian sound that shaped European music for generations. Works by Vivaldi and Albinoni sit beside pieces by Castello, Handel, Maria Teresa Agnesi and Antonio Archilei, whose song "Dalle più alte sfere" is one of the highlights.
## What to listen for

Handel's cantata Armida abbandonata puts the spotlight on the soprano Amanda Forsythe, a GRAMMY-winning singer who joins the ensemble for the concerts. The viola da gamba player Cristiano Contadin brings the warm, grounded tone of that instrument to the repertoire, which suits the intimate scale of the X-tet.

A folk-inspired Tarantella Gargano adds a dance-like lift to the middle of the program. The evening closes with Morgantina Studies, a new work by the composer Colin Jacobsen, which carries the program from centuries-old Italian sources into a contemporary voice.
## Dates, venue and tickets

The two concerts are on Friday, Nov. 13 and Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, at Seully Hall, Boston Conservatory at Berklee. The season page we checked does not list start times or a street address for the hall, so check the listing before you go. It gives no ticket prices either. It does say that subscriptions and memberships bring savings, so the ensemble's own site is the place to start.
If the X-tet concerts whet your appetite, Boston Baroque's season continues with Handel's Messiah on Dec. 12 and 13 at Jordan Hall, a classic way to spend a December evening with baroque music.

title: A Saturday Recital at Club Passim Showcases the School of Music

body: On Saturday, November 14, Club Passim opens its doors at 11 AM for a Passim School of Music recital, with the show starting at noon. Passim is one of the area's best-known listening rooms, and an early-afternoon recital is a rare chance to hear the school's work up close.

The listing tags the program with roots and traditional styles: Americana, bluegrass, Celtic, fiddle, old-time and singer-songwriter music. Performers and repertoire are not named on the page, which makes the afternoon a pleasant surprise for anyone who loves the sound of a roomful of strings.
## About the school

Passim School of Music offers classes, workshops and one-on-one lessons with instructors, and the recital is a window into what happens in those rooms. For parents thinking about lessons, or adults who have always wanted to pick up an instrument, an hour in the audience is a fine way to hear what the school teaches.
## Tickets and getting there

General admission is $15, and members are admitted at no charge. The listing also notes a $3 processing fee and a $2 preservation fee per ticket, with the processing fee waived at the box office. Club Passim sits in Harvard Square, a short walk from Harvard station on the Red Line.
Afternoon shows make it easy to pair a recital with lunch or a stroll around the Square before the music starts.

title: Tufts Choirs Bring Brahms's German Requiem to Medford, Nov. 15
dek: Sunday, Nov. 15 at 3:00 PM at the Granoff Music Center's Distler Hall in Medford: the Tufts Concert Choir and Chamber Singers, with no charge admission.
body: The Tufts University Concert Choir and Chamber Singers present a Sunday afternoon of choral music on November 15, 2026, at 3:00 PM in the Distler Performance Hall of the Granoff Music Center, 20 Talbot Avenue in Medford. The concert is conducted by Jamie Kirsch and accompanied by pianists Thomas Stumpf and Edith Auner, and the listing gives an end time of 4:30 PM.
## What you will hear

The program includes selections from Brahms's A German Requiem, a large-scale work for chorus that Brahms wrote for the consolation of the living, alongside music by Jenkins, Esmail, Wright and Dello Joio.
Brahms wrote the work in German rather than Latin, and the Tufts program offers a chance to hear its choral writing in a university setting.
## Admission and planning

Brahms completed A German Requiem over several years, and the full work was first performed in Bremen in 1868. Its texts are drawn from the Lutheran Bible rather than the Latin Mass, which sets it apart from the requiem settings most listeners know.

Admission is no charge. The listing does not say whether reservations are needed, so check the Tufts event page before heading out. The concert is a good afternoon for anyone who wants to hear a university choir and its chamber singers in a hall built for music.

title: Jenna Moynihan and Owen Marshall Play Club Passim, Nov. 15
dek: Sunday, November 15, with doors at 1:00 PM and the show at 2:00 PM at Club Passim in Cambridge.
body: On Sunday, November 15, Jenna Moynihan and Owen Marshall play Club Passim in Cambridge. Doors open at 1:00 PM and the show starts at 2:00 PM, which makes this an easy afternoon outing for anyone who loves Celtic and traditional music.

Moynihan is a freestyle fiddler whose playing draws mainly on Scottish tradition, with influences from American, Irish and Swedish music. She has toured with several acts, has performed as a soloist with the Boston Pops, and teaches internationally. She is an assistant professor of strings at Berklee College of Music.

Marshall is a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, mandolin and banjo, and he is known for his bouzouki playing and melodic guitar work. He has toured and recorded with groups including the Seamus Egan Project and Dervish, and he has long accompanied traditional musicians.
Tickets are $35 general admission and $33 for members, sold through the ticket link on the Passim event page. The listing does not state a separate reservation requirement.
Because the set begins early in the afternoon, it also pairs well with the evening show by Lucy Kaplansky, which Passim lists the same day.

title: Lysander Piano Trio Plays Grieg and Dvořák at the Gardner, Nov. 15
dek: Sunday, Nov. 15, from 1:30 to 3:30 p.m. in Calderwood Hall at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way.
body: The Lysander Piano Trio plays Calderwood Hall on Sunday, Nov. 15, from 1:30 to 3:30 p.m. as part of the Gardner's Fall 2026 Weekend Concert Series, which the listing describes as a ten-concert season.
## The program

The program includes works by Amanda Maier, Edvard Grieg and Antonín Dvořák. It also features Bongani Ndodana-Breen's Two Nguni Dances, which draws on sub-Saharan traditions, including those of the composer's Xhosa heritage.

The listing says the program centers on Maier, a Swedish violinist-composer who worked with Brahms and Grieg. The Gardner is at 25 Evans Way in Boston, 02115, and the afternoon concert runs from 1:30 to 3:30 p.m.
## The ensemble
According to the listing, the trio met as students at Juilliard. The Washington Post praised the group for "an uncommon degree of heart-on-the-sleeve emotional frankness."
## The hall

Calderwood Hall is a 300-seat room, and most of its seats are in the front row, per the listing. The Weekend Concert Series dates to 1927, and the listing calls it the longest-running museum music program in the country.

Tickets are listed at $70 to $99, with seniors at $63 to $89 and students and children ages 5 to 17 at $25.

title: Dover Quartet Brings Brahms and Dvorak to Jordan Hall, Nov. 15
dek: Sunday, Nov. 15 at 3 p.m. at NEC's Jordan Hall in the Fenway, presented by Vivo Performing Arts with Brahms, Dvorak and Pura Fe.
body: Few chamber ensembles bring the sense of occasion that the Dover Quartet brings to a program built from three very different string quartets. On Sunday, Nov. 15, at 3 p.m., the group performs at NEC's Jordan Hall in the Fenway. Vivo Performing Arts presents the concert as an Aaron Richmond Recital, named for the organization's founder.
## The program

The afternoon opens with Johannes Brahms's String Quartet No. 3 in B-flat major, Op. 67, written in 1875 and running about 34 minutes across four movements. Next comes Rattle Songs by Pura Fe, the Indigenous singer-songwriter, in an orchestration by the Chickasaw composer Jerod Impichchaachaaha' Tate. The concert closes with Antonin Dvorak's String Quartet No. 11 in C major, Op. 61, a warm and sweeping work of about 35 minutes.
## The players

The quartet is made up of violinists Bryan Lee and Adam Barnett-Hart, violist Julianne Lee and cellist Camden Shaw. The event page notes that Barnett-Hart is replacing the listed first violinist, Joel Link, for this engagement. Barnett-Hart is a founding member of the Escher String Quartet, a former BBC New Generation Artist and a recipient of the Avery Fisher Career Grant, according to the page.
## Getting there

Jordan Hall sits on the New England Conservatory campus. Tickets are sold online through the Vivo event page, which also lists 35 Under tickets through its app and member access. The page does not list ticket prices, so check the box office before you go.

The page praises the quartet's refined, luminous playing. Setting two late-nineteenth-century masterpieces beside a contemporary voice from the Indigenous tradition makes the afternoon feel like a conversation across generations, and it is a fine reason to spend a Sunday in the Fenway.

title: Last Call for 'Wicked' at the Citizens Opera House: Closes Nov. 15
dek: The Broadway blockbuster's fall run on Washington Street ends in just over two weeks.
body: If you have been meaning to see Wicked in Boston this fall, the clock is ticking. Broadway In Boston's run of the musical at the Citizens Opera House ends Sunday, Nov. 15, after opening Sept. 23.

The show, which tells the backstory of the witches of Oz before Dorothy ever drops in, remains one of the most reliable crowd-pleasers on the touring circuit, with a big score, big sets and one of the best-known first-act closers in musical theater. It came to town as an add-on to the 2026/27 Broadway In Boston subscription season, so single tickets have been the main way in.
## The details

The Citizens Opera House is at 539 Washington St. in Downtown Crossing, a short walk from the Orange and Red lines at Downtown Crossing and the Green Line at Boylston. Tickets are sold through Broadway In Boston. With closing weekend approaching, the best seat selection is usually on weeknights.
## What comes next in the Theater District

The Opera House stage turns over quickly. Boston Ballet moves in with The Nutcracker on Nov. 27, and Broadway In Boston's subscription season continues at the Emerson Colonial Theatre with The Notebook, Dec. 8 to 20. In the new year, Death Becomes Her plays the Opera House Jan. 12 to 24, followed by Maybe Happy Ending, Feb. 2 to 14.

title: Snowport Returns to the Seaport With 130 Makers and Live Music
dek: Opens Friday, Nov. 6, at 100 Seaport Boulevard in the Seaport District, with weekend hours from 10 a.m. and the market running through Dec. 27.
body: Snowport, the holiday market that has become a fixture of Boston's Seaport District, opened its sixth season on Friday, Nov. 6, at 100 Seaport Boulevard. More than 130 independent businesses are taking part, including 17 local food and beverage vendors, and Boston 25 News reports that most of them are based in New England.

Shoppers will find apparel, jewelry, home decor, artwork, toys, gourmet gifts and other items from local makers. Boston.com's listing adds a separate Christmas tree market, which opens Nov. 20, according to NBC Boston, iceless curling that can be reserved through Feb. 28, 2027, and photo spots. Live music is back this season: Mohegan Music Mondays features emerging Boston-area performers from Berklee College of Music starting at 5 p.m. each Monday, and more music is planned from Tuesday through Thursday, according to Boston 25.
## Hours and entry

General admission is no charge. From Nov. 6 through Dec. 6 the market is open Monday through Thursday from 3 to 8 p.m., Friday from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., Saturday from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Weekday hours start at 11 a.m. from Dec. 7. The market is closed on Thanksgiving and Christmas Day and closes at 6 p.m. on Christmas Eve. Weekend timed-entry passes are reserved through the Seaport Insider app, at $15 for adults, according to Boston 25.
## Beyond the stalls

The market also includes a Creativity Corner for craft projects such as snow globe making, as WBUR's weekend preview describes it. The holiday calendar continues on Dec. 4 at 6 p.m., when a tree lighting takes place at 85 Northern Avenue, and a menorah lighting follows on Dec. 10 at 6 p.m. at 60 Seaport Boulevard, according to Boston.com.

Snowport is a reminder that the holiday season in Boston does not have to be spent in one crowded hall. For an afternoon it offers a gift from a local studio, a student's set on a Monday evening, and a chance to make something by hand before the lights go up across the city. The market runs through Dec. 27, so there is time to return.

title: Friday Organ Recitals at Trinity Church in Copley Square
dek: Fridays at 12:15 p.m. on Nov. 6, 13 and 20 at Trinity Church, 206 Clarendon St., Back Bay.
body: Trinity Church in Copley Square is hosting a series of midday organ recitals this November. Each one is held on a Friday at 12:15 p.m., which makes it an easy break from a busy workday or a relaxed stop on a fall afternoon.

The recitals fall on November 6, 13 and 20. Admission is no charge, and the church suggests a $10 donation toward the music program. The series offers a quiet half hour of organ music inside one of the city's great interiors.

Trinity Church was designed by the architect H. H. Richardson and completed in the 1870s, and it is among the most celebrated buildings in Boston. Its stained glass and carved woodwork make the sanctuary an ideal setting for organ music, and few places in the city pair architecture and sound this well.
## Plan Your Visit

The church is at 206 Clarendon Street, on the Copley Square side of Back Bay, and is an easy walk from Copley station on the Green Line. Arrive a few minutes early to find a seat. The schedule and recital details are posted at https://trinitychurchboston.org/music/organ-recitals/

title: MBTA Opens No-Fare Pilot for Riders 75 and Older Who Stopped Driving
dek: Enrollment opened Oct. 13 for older residents who have given up the car keys; here is how to sign up.
body: Older Bostonians who have handed in their car keys can now ride the T without paying a fare. Enrollment in a new MBTA pilot program opened Oct. 13 for Massachusetts residents age 75 and older who no longer drive.

The program is a joint effort of the MBTA and the Registry of Motor Vehicles, and it covers the whole system: buses, subway, ferries and Commuter Rail. It is part of a broader package of fare-relief measures for riders announced over the summer.
## Who qualifies

Applicants must be Massachusetts residents, at least 75, and must hold a Massachusetts ID card, the state ID that does not carry driving privileges. Anyone who does not have one yet can apply for it through the RMV first.
## How to sign up

There are two ways in. The online application lets riders have the credential mailed or pick it up in person. Or go straight to the Charlie Service Center at 296 Washington St., between Milk and Water streets, close to State Street and Downtown Crossing stations. The center is fully accessible, and walk-in applicants get a temporary credential the same day, with the permanent one following by mail.

The state has not announced an end date for the pilot. For families helping a parent or grandparent, the in-person route is the quickest way to walk out with a working pass.

Joe Lovano and Melissa Aldana play tenor saxophone. Leo Genovese is on piano, Linda May Han Oh plays bass and Jeff 'Tain' Watts is on drums. Together they present the concert as a collective tribute rather than a single-artist show.

body: Singer-songwriters Laurie MacAllister and Seth Glier share a bill at Club Passim on Saturday, Nov. 21. Doors open at 7:00 PM and the show starts at 8:00 PM.
## Laurie MacAllister

MacAllister co-founded the Americana trio Red Molly, which released seven albums. She launched a solo career in late 2024 with a show at Club Passim. Her 2018 solo album, The Lies the Poets Tell, pays tribute to the contemporary folk scene.
## Seth Glier

Glier is a Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist. His sixth album, The Coronation, was released on MPress Records. He has won five Independent Music Awards and has performed with James Taylor and Ani DiFranco.

title: Quincy Market Tree Lighting on Nov. 21 Brings Santa to Faneuil Hall
dek: Saturday, Nov. 21, from 2:00 to 6:00 PM at Quincy Market in Faneuil Hall, with the tree lighting at 6:00 PM.
body: Downtown's holiday season starts at Quincy Market on Saturday, Nov. 21, when Faneuil Hall Marketplace holds its annual tree lighting. The celebration runs from 2:00 to 6:00 PM, and the tree lights at 6:00 PM.

The listing says Make-A-Wish and Santa will take part, which makes the afternoon an easy outing for families. Admission is at no charge, and the listing does not mention any registration, so you can simply arrive.
## A little history

The market building dates to 1826 and takes its name from Josiah Quincy, the Boston mayor who oversaw its construction. Today the hall is a busy downtown landmark, and its food and gift stalls make it an easy place to spend an afternoon.
## Bring the family

The afternoon suits a relaxed visit with children. The tree gives the day a clear focal point, and the 6:00 PM lighting brings the event to its close, so you can time a walk through the market to end at the tree.
## Before you go

The listing does not give a street address, so Quincy Market in the Faneuil Hall area of downtown Boston is the place to head. Plan to arrive a little before 6:00 PM if you want to see the lighting itself. Faneuil Hall Marketplace organizes the event, and its listing is the best place to check for any change to the schedule before you go.

title: Convivium's A North Atlantic Christmas Comes to All Saints in Brookline
dek: Saturday, Nov. 21, from 7:00 to 8:30 PM at All Saints Parish, 1773 Beacon Street in Brookline, with tickets at $25.
body: On Saturday evening, Nov. 21, the ensemble Convivium presents A North Atlantic Christmas at All Saints Parish in Brookline. The concert runs from 7:00 to 8:30 PM at 1773 Beacon Street and is built around Christmas and devotional music from both sides of the Atlantic.
## The program

The first part of the program brings English Christmas pieces by Tallis and Byrd. It then turns to villancicos and motets from Portugal, Spain and Mexico City, including Victoria's O Magnum Mysterium. The program also includes works by early New England composers Billings and Ingalls.
## A little history

William Billings, a Boston composer of the late 1700s, published hymn collections that helped shape choral singing in New England. Putting his work beside the older European repertoire shows how the same sacred texts were set in very different places.
## Tickets
Admission is $25. The listing does not describe how to buy tickets or register, so check convivium.org for details before you go.

Convivium is the ensemble behind the concert, and its listing points to convivium.org for more about the group and its season. This is a concert for listeners who like their holiday music a little older than the usual sleigh bells, and who enjoy hearing carols and motets sung in their original languages.

title: Peter and the Wolf Gets a Family Concert at Symphony Hall, Nov. 21

body: The Boston Youth Symphony Orchestras and the Boston Ballet School present Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf at Symphony Hall on Saturday, Nov. 21, at 12:00 PM. The event is part of the BSO's family concert series.

Federico Cortese is listed as music director of the Boston Youth Symphony Orchestras, and Tamara King as associate director of the Boston Ballet School. The page describes the work as a symphony fairy tale in which each character is given its own tune on a specific instrument.

The story follows adventure, teamwork, bravery and compassion, and the page offers the bird as the flute and the cat as the clarinet as examples of how the instruments are matched to the characters. It is an easy first concert for young listeners.

title: Jan Lisiecki Plays Mendelssohn at Symphony Hall, Nov. 19-21
dek: Pianist Jan Lisiecki joins conductor Samy Rachid and the BSO Nov. 19, 20 and 21 at Symphony Hall on Massachusetts Avenue.
body: After a week of oratorio and world premiere, the Boston Symphony Orchestra turns to the lyrical heart of the Romantic repertoire. Pianist Jan Lisiecki plays Mendelssohn's Piano Concerto No. 1, framed by Weber and Schumann, in a program led by conductor Samy Rachid.

The program is part of the BSO's 2026-27 season under Music Director Andris Nelsons, which runs from Sept. 18 to May 9. It arrives between two weeks of the orchestra's Creation festival and a late-November program with pianist Jean-Yves Thibaudet, making it the quieter, more traditional stop in a busy month at Symphony Hall.
## The program
The evening opens with the overture to Weber's Oberon. Lisiecki then takes the solo part in Mendelssohn's Piano Concerto No. 1. The concert ends with Schumann's Symphony No. 1, nicknamed Spring.
## The artists

Marc Mandel's Friday talk is a good way to get oriented before the Schumann, and the Friday afternoon time suits listeners who prefer a daytime concert. Thursday and Saturday are evening performances, so there is a choice of schedules whether you are visiting from out of town or live nearby.
Jan Lisiecki is the soloist, and Samy Rachid conducts the Boston Symphony Orchestra.
## Dates and times
Performances at Symphony Hall are Thursday, Nov. 19 at 7:30 p.m.; Friday, Nov. 20 at 1:30 p.m., preceded by a talk by Marc Mandel from 12:15 to 12:45 p.m.; and Saturday, Nov. 21 at 8 p.m.
## Tickets and location

Symphony Hall is at 301 Massachusetts Avenue, Boston, MA 02115. Each performance has its own Buy Tickets link on the BSO's event page; single-ticket prices are not published there. Subscription packages that include this program start at $231. For questions call 617-266-1200 (Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Saturday, 12:30 to 4:30 p.m.) or email customerservice@bso.org.
It is a classic Romantic program, three well-loved composers in one concert at Symphony Hall.

title: Kapilow and A Far Cry Unpack Mozart's Clarinet Concerto, Nov. 22
dek: Sunday, Nov. 22 at 3:00 PM at NEC's Jordan Hall in Fenway: Rob Kapilow, A Far Cry and clarinetist Romie de Guise-Langlois take on Mozart's Clarinet Concerto.
body: Rob Kapilow's What Makes It Great? series returns to Jordan Hall on Sunday, November 22, at 3:00 PM, presented by Vivo Performing Arts. This installment takes up Mozart's Clarinet Concerto, a late work, with A Far Cry and clarinetist Romie de Guise-Langlois joining Kapilow on stage.

The series is built on close listening. Kapilow, a music educator, combines detailed analysis with storytelling and humor, and the afternoon pairs an in-depth look at the concerto with a performance of it.
## Who is performing
A Far Cry, which the organization describes as Boston's A Far Cry chamber orchestra, presents concerts, touring, recordings and education programs. Romie de Guise-Langlois is the clarinet soloist.
Jordan Hall, home of the New England Conservatory, is one of the city's principal chamber music halls, and the listing gives a 3:00 PM start.
## Where and how to buy

The concert takes place at NEC's Jordan Hall, 290 Huntington Avenue, Boston. The event lists several price levels, and tickets are available through the Get Tickets button on the Vivo page. Questions about programming or ticketing can go to 617-482-6661 or boxoffice@vivoperformingarts.org.

Mozart wrote the Clarinet Concerto in 1791, the last year of his life, and it has become one of the most loved works in the clarinet repertoire. For listeners who know the piece well, a guided hearing can bring out details that a concert performance alone may pass over.
For listeners who want to know what they are hearing, the afternoon offers a concerto explained before it is played in full.

title: Masterworks Chorale Sings Mozart's Coronation Mass, Nov. 22
dek: Sunday, Nov. 22 from 3:00 to 5:00 PM at Cary Memorial Hall in Lexington: Masterworks Chorale, Kevin Leong and the Pro Arte Chamber Orchestra.
body: Masterworks Chorale opens a Sunday afternoon of Mozart and the Haydns on November 22, 2026, from 3:00 to 5:00 PM at Cary Memorial Hall, 1605 Massachusetts Avenue in Lexington. Music Director Kevin Leong leads the chorale, which is joined by soloists Deborah Selig, soprano; Roselin Osser, mezzo-soprano; Gregory Zavracky, tenor; and Will Prapestis, baritone, and by the Pro Arte Chamber Orchestra.
## The program

Mozart's Coronation Mass is the featured work. The program also includes Mozart's Dixit et Magnificat, Joseph Haydn's Responsoria, and Michael Haydn's Timete Dominum and Beatus vir, so the afternoon sets the two composers' sacred music side by side.
## About the chorale

Mozart completed the Coronation Mass in 1779 while working in Salzburg, and the afternoon pairs it with other sacred works from the same circle of composers, so audiences can hear how the music of the period was built for the church.

The group was founded in 1940 as the Lexington Choral Society and renamed Masterworks Chorale in 1969 to reflect its geographically diverse membership. Allen Lannom conducted the chorus from 1952 to 2005, and Steven Karidoyanes became Music Director in 2006.
The Pro Arte Chamber Orchestra accompanies the choral works, so the sound is full-scale rather than a single keyboard. The concert runs about two hours, from 3:00 to 5:00 PM.
## Tickets

Saturday, November 14 at 8:00 PM; Sunday, November 15 at 2:00 PM; Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21 at 8:00 PM; and Sunday, November 22 at 2:00 PM.
The festival runs across two weekends, with Friday and Saturday evening shows and Sunday afternoon performances, so the schedule suits both weeknight and weekend audiences.
## What the plays explore
The plays look at how people perform in their daily lives and how they keep going when life is disrupted. Some pieces also give audiences a look backstage.

Festivals of short plays give a community theater company a chance to try many voices in one evening. Each piece tells its own story, so audiences can see a range of work without committing to a full-length production.

title: Oriana Consort Sings Tennyson, Folk Songs and Poulenc, Nov. 22
dek: Sunday, Nov. 22 at 5:00 PM at First Lutheran Church on Berkeley Street in Back Bay: the Oriana Consort's fall concert.
body: The Oriana Consort, a chorale of about 25 adult mixed voices directed by Walter Chapin, gives its fall concert at First Lutheran Church, 299 Berkeley Street, on Sunday, November 22, at 5:00 PM. The listing runs to about 7:00 PM.
## The program

Two settings of Tennyson's The Lotos-Eaters, by Robert Hobby and Daniel Gawthorp, open each half of the concert. Between them come British Isles folk songs by Gawthorp, Ralph Vaughan Williams, Alice Parker and Ēriks Ešenvalds, French songs by Debussy, Saint-Saëns and Poulenc, and sacred works by Salamone Rossi, Randall Thompson, Charles Villiers Stanford, Williametta Spencer, Ešenvalds and Rosephanye Powell.

Tennyson's poem describes sailors who settle into a languid island life, and the concert opens with two settings of it. The program then moves from English poetry to folk song, French art song and sacred music, a range that suits a chorale of about 25 voices.
## About the group
Founded in 1994 and based in Cambridge, the Oriana Consort aims for what it describes as a warm, attractive and compelling choral sound.
The listing gives an end time of about 7:00 PM, so the concert fits an early Sunday evening. The church sits in Back Bay near Copley Square.

body: Ballet BC, the Vancouver company led by artistic director Medhi Walerski, comes to Boston this month for two performances at the Cutler Majestic Theatre at Emerson College. The Saturday show, Nov. 21, begins at 8:00 PM. A Sunday afternoon performance, Nov. 22, also runs; confirm its start time on the Vivo Performing Arts listing before you go.

Presented by Vivo Performing Arts, the program is described as an evening about tenderness, ecstasy and human longing, danced by a company of 20 dancers. The listing does not name the individual works or their choreographers, so the program itself is the surprise. What it does promise is a contemporary idiom in which movement carries the story.
## A Vancouver company on a Boston stage

This visit brings the company's work to a Boston audience that has a long tradition of ballet, with the Boston Ballet's seasons at the Boston Opera House and the Nutcracker that fills the calendar each winter. Ballet BC offers a different experience. Its contemporary repertory is built around dancers who move with weight, speed and emotional directness, and a single evening lets a viewer see a full company rather than a few guest soloists.

The listing's focus on tenderness and longing points to a program that is as much about feeling as technique. For a program built on physical expression, the scale of the house matters. The Cutler Majestic is a smaller theatre than the big civic halls, so the dancers are close enough that the emotional arc of the evening should read clearly from most seats.
## Where to see it and how to get tickets

The Cutler Majestic Theatre is at 219 Tremont Street, on the Emerson College campus. Single tickets are sold through Vivo Performing Arts, which lists multiple price points. An Applause Circle membership, $25, gives early access to tickets, with details at vivoarts.org/applause-circle. Plan for the Saturday show at 8:00 PM or the Sunday afternoon performance, and check the Vivo listing for the Sunday start time before you buy.

title: Zander Conducts Bruckner's Fifth at Symphony Hall, Nov. 22
dek: Benjamin Zander leads the Boston Philharmonic Orchestra in Schubert and Bruckner Sunday, Nov. 22 at 3 p.m., Symphony Hall, Back Bay.
body: Some concerts are worth planning around because of what is on the stage: a conductor who loves the music, and a symphony the orchestra has almost never played. On Sunday, Nov. 22, Benjamin Zander leads the Boston Philharmonic Orchestra in Schubert's Unfinished Symphony and Bruckner's Symphony No. 5.
## What you will hear

Schubert's Symphony No. 8, the Unfinished, runs about 25 minutes. Zander counts it among his favorite works. No one knows why Schubert left it unfinished, since he lived six more years after writing it, and it remains one of the most beloved works in the repertoire.

Bruckner's Fifth, about 81 minutes long, is the main event. The orchestra describes it as a magnificent, heaven-storming symphony of overwhelming grandeur, and notes that the Philharmonic has played it only once in its nearly 50-year history. It is a rare chance to hear it live.
## Why now
The Boston Philharmonic is presenting its final season at Symphony Hall, according to a WBUR fall concert guide.
## Details
The concert begins at 3 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 22. A guide to the music with Zander begins at 1:45 p.m. Symphony Hall is at 301 Massachusetts Avenue, Boston, MA 02115.

Tickets are sold through the orchestra's website at bostonphil.org and the BSO's ticketing page for the performance. Ticket prices are not listed on either page. For phone help with BSO ticketing, call 617-266-1200 (Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; Saturday, 12:30 to 4:30 p.m.).
A beloved symphony and a rarely performed one make a fitting pairing.
